# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Data missingness shows up in many real-life scenarios, arising from different sources like improper data collection, malfunctioning equipment, or operational data loss. In all these scenarios, imputation, which is the process of filling data gaps with estimated values, is a widely accepted approach to complete missing data for machine learning and deep-learning tasks such as classification and regression. For instance, biomedical data frequently suffers from extensive missingness due to patient behavior, poor data management, and biased sampling, which complicates downstream analyses like patient stratification. <!-- imputation is the process of replacing values with estimated values, make connection between missiing data in real life and known techniques in ML. Be more explicit about what kind of downstream task -->

However, it is well-known that all types of imputation induce biases in the data that can negatively impact the downstream task, and recent work has shown that improvements in the quality of imputation do not necessarily result in improvement in downstream task performance. In particular, the quality of imputation decreases when the size of the dataset is small. In this thesis, I will focus on datasets with small sample sizes, which for example arise very often in biomedical contexts. Small datasets can in particular reduce the quality of simple imputation due to sampling error, especially in the case of heterogenous features. <!--Write about focus on small heterogenous data, for example genomic data.-->

In this thesis, I argue that nearest neighbour-based imputation methods can outperform advanced deep neural network-based and generative approaches. In particular, I derive theoretical guarantees for \acr{kNN} imputation under different missingness scenarios, and modify the \acr{kNN} imputation paradigm by introducing a novel loss function that still allows us to maintain those theoretical guarantees. AFurthermore, I show that jointly training a hyperparameter-tunable loss function that forms a homotopy between the imputation and downstream objectives can further improve downstream task performance, thereby going beyond the conventional impute-then-classify paradigm. I also consider settings where the missingnes is structurally regular, such as in short multivariate time series with missing timepoints or missing features. For these problems I demonstrate that discretization-invariant feature extraction and classification based on functional data analysis techniques can outperform the classical impute-then-extract features paradigm. Finally, I extend the discussion of missingness to missing labels in more complex structured data, such as graph-structured datasets, wihtin the same missingness framework used in imputation literature. I show how the inherent local and global community structure of the network can be used to construct informative node features for imputing the missing labels, in a more accurate and computationally efficient manner than random walk or mutual information-based formulations.

These results demonstrate that imputation quality alone should not be the sole criterion for evaluating and constructing missing-data methods. Since imputation is ultimately performed to facilitate downstream analysis, the objectives of the downstream task should be explicitly incorporated into the design and evaluation of imputation methods. This can be achieved either by jointly optimizing imputation and downstream objectives, as in the proposed loss-based \acr{kNN} approach, or by bypassing imputation altogether when the structure of the data permits, as in the functional data analysis-based approach. More broadly, this thesis advocates for a task-oriented perspective on missing data, in which the success of an imputation method is ultimately determined not only by how accurately it reconstructs missing values, but also by how effectively it supports the downstream task.
